beats.text: A key you never use. A {caps}Caps Lock that gets in the way. Mouse buttons that {side}do nothing in your game. Let's put them to work.
We'll {how}see how K-Board works, {real}look at a real profile, and {tip}switch it on with a single key.
{kboard}K-Board changes what your keys and mouse buttons actually do.
You edit a profile on a {drawn}drawn keyboard and mouse. {click}Click a key, {choose}choose what it becomes, and it {lights}lights up with its new job.
A key can become {key}another key, a {combo}combination, a piece of {text}text, one of your {command}commands, or {nothing}nothing at all.
{caps}Caps Lock as Control. The {win}Windows key disabled while you play. The {side}side buttons as copy and paste.
With {modifiers}modifiers, you get layers: {ctrlj}Control plus J can do something completely different from {j}J.
A profile can work {everywhere}everywhere, or only in {apps}certain apps. And you switch it on and off from a {command}command, or from the {tray}tray icon.

Here's a real one: {gaming}Gaming, only for {elden}Elden Ring. {caps}Caps Lock becomes Shift. The {win}Windows key does nothing. {f1}F1 runs a command that mutes the microphone. The {side}side buttons become R and F. And {f12}F12 types gg wp.
To add one, click {press}Press key, and press the key, button or combination you want to change.
One last tip: a {command}command can switch a profile {toggle}on and off. Give it a {hotkey}hotkey, and your whole gaming setup is {one}one key away.
